KIPLMC/Geometry.lean.title: The scaled particle potential and its gradient
KIPLMC/Geometry.lean.summary:
Throughout this report \(d_ heta,d_x\ge0\) and \(N\ge0\) are integers and \(U:\mathbb R^{d_ heta} imes\mathbb R^{d_x} o\mathbb R\) is a joint potential of a parameter \( heta\) and a latent variable \(x\); in the statistical application \(U( heta,x)=-\log p_ heta(x,y)\) for fixed data \(y\). The product \(\mathbb R^{d_ heta} imes\mathbb R^{d_x}\) carries the Euclidean norm \(\|( heta,x)\|^2=\| heta\|^2+\|x\|^2\). The particle state space is \(\mathcal Z_N=\mathbb R^{d_ heta} imes(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\), with points \(z=( heta,z_1,\dots,z_N)\) and Euclidean norm \(\|z\|^2=\| heta\|^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\|z_i\|^2\); it has dimension \(d_ heta+Nd_x\). The block \(z_i\) stands for \(X^i/\sqrt N\), where \(X^i\in\mathbb R^{d_x}\) is the latent variable of particle \(i\), and the linear map \(J_i(z)=( heta,\sqrt Nz_i)\) recovers the physical pair \(( heta,X^i)\).

This section studies the lifted potential \(V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU(J_iz)\), the averaged potential \( ar U_N=N^{-1}V_N\) and the force \(F_N=N^{-1} abla V_N\). We prove that \(F_N= abla ar U_N\); that \( ar U_N\) is \(m\)-strongly convex whenever \(U\) is, and that \(F_N\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz whenever \( abla U\) is, with the same constants \(m\) and \(L\) for every \(N>0\); and that the parameter block of \(F_N\) is the particle average of \( abla_ heta U( heta,X^i)\), while the latent block multiplied by \(\sqrt N\) is the unaveraged gradient \( abla_xU( heta,X^i)\). The force \(F_N\) drives the kinetic particle diffusion and both particle algorithms of this report, and the constants \(m,L\) enter every convergence estimate.

steps.title: The particle state space, the averaged potential and the force
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(I_N\) be the disjoint union of \(\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\) and \(\{1,\dots,N\}\times\{1,\dots,d_x\}\), and let \(\mathcal Z_N=\mathbb R^{I_N}\) with the inner product \(\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_{a\in I_N}z_aw_a\). The parameter block of \(z\) is \(\theta=(z_j)_{j\le d_\theta}\) and the \(i\)th latent block is \(z_i=(z_{(i,j)})_{j\le d_x}\). For \(U:\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\to\mathbb R\) and \(z\in\mathcal Z_N\) define

\[V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^NU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i),\qquad\bar U_N(z)=N^{-1}V_N(z),\qquad F_N(z)=N^{-1}\nabla V_N(z),\]

where \(N^{-1}\) is read as \(0\) when \(N=0\). For \(N=0\) the sum is empty, so \(V_0=\bar U_0=0\) and \(F_0=0\).

Gradient. If \(f:\mathcal Z_N\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(z\), its derivative \(Df(z)\) is a linear functional on the finite-dimensional inner product space \(\mathcal Z_N\). By the Riesz representation theorem there is a unique vector \(\nabla f(z)\) with

\[\langle\nabla f(z),w\rangle=Df(z)[w]\qquad\text{for every }w\in\mathcal Z_N;\]

in coordinates \(\nabla f(z)_a=\partial_af(z)\). Where \(f\) is not differentiable the gradient is defined to be \(0\); this convention plays no role below, because every potential to which it is applied is differentiable.

Interpretation. Writing \(X^i=\sqrt Nz_i\), one has \(J_iz=(\theta,X^i)\), \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,X^i)\) and \(\|z\|^2=\|\theta\|^2+N^{-1}\sum_i\|X^i\|^2\). The maps \(J_i:\mathcal Z_N\to\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), \(J_i(z)=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\), are linear, and for every \(w\in\mathcal Z_N\) with parameter block \(w_\theta\),

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_iw\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl(\|w_\theta\|^2+N\|w_i\|^2\bigr)=N\Bigl(\|w_\theta\|^2+\sum_{i=1}^N\|w_i\|^2\Bigr)=N\|w\|^2.\]

This norm identity is used in the next steps. The parameter block is copied into all \(N\) pairs, which produces the factor \(N\) in front of \(\|w_\theta\|^2\); the latent blocks carry the factor \(\sqrt N\) inside \(J_i\), which produces the same factor in front of \(\|w_i\|^2\). The two contributions therefore combine into \(N\|w\|^2\), and dividing \(V_N\) by \(N\) removes this factor from the curvature constants.

steps.title: The force is the gradient of the averaged potential
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be differentiable on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\) and let \(N\ge0\). Then \(\bar U_N\) is differentiable and

\[\nabla\bar U_N(z)=F_N(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z_N.\]

If \(N>0\), then moreover \(V_N(z)=N\,\bar U_N(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathcal Z_N\).

Proof. Each \(J_i\) is linear, hence differentiable with derivative \(J_i\) at every point, so by the chain rule \(z\mapsto U(J_iz)\) is differentiable with derivative \(w\mapsto DU(J_iz)[J_iw]\). A finite sum of differentiable functions is differentiable; hence \(V_N\) is differentiable, which is the differentiability statement of the particle geometry (). By the rule for constant multiples, \(\bar U_N=N^{-1}V_N\) is differentiable and

\[D\bar U_N(z)[w]=N^{-1}\,DV_N(z)[w]\qquad(w\in\mathcal Z_N).\qquad(1)\]

Fix \(z\) and an arbitrary \(w\in\mathcal Z_N\). By the defining property of \(\nabla\bar U_N(z)\), identity (1), the defining property of \(\nabla V_N(z)\) and linearity of the inner product in its first argument,

\[\langle\nabla\bar U_N(z),w\rangle=D\bar U_N(z)[w]=N^{-1}DV_N(z)[w]=N^{-1}\langle\nabla V_N(z),w\rangle=\langle F_N(z),w\rangle.\]

Hence \(u=\nabla\bar U_N(z)-F_N(z)\) satisfies \(\langle u,w\rangle=0\) for every \(w\). Taking \(w=u\) gives \(\|u\|^2=0\), so \(u=0\).

For the second statement, \(N>0\) means that the real number \(N\) is nonzero, so \(N\cdot N^{-1}=1\) and

\[N\,\bar U_N(z)=N\bigl(N^{-1}V_N(z)\bigr)=(N\cdot N^{-1})\,V_N(z)=V_N(z).\qquad\square\]

When \(N=0\) both sides of the gradient identity vanish, so that identity needs no hypothesis on \(N\). The force \(F_N\) is thus a gradient field, which is what allows the kinetic theory for a potential \(f\) to be applied with \(f=\bar U_N\); the identity \(V_N=N\bar U_N\) converts between the averaged normalization and the sum normalization used for the rescaled dynamics later in the report.

steps.title: Averaging preserves the strong convexity constant
steps.body:
Strong convexity. Let \(m\in\mathbb R\). A function \(f\) on a real inner product space \(E\) is \(m\)-strongly convex if for all \(x,y\in E\) and all \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\),

\[f(ax+by)\le af(x)+bf(y)-ab\,\frac m2\,\|x-y\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

For \(m=0\) this is convexity. For differentiable \(f\) and \(m>0\) it is equivalent to the monotonicity condition \(\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\ge m\|x-y\|^2\), which is the form of Assumption H1 in the paper; this equivalence is not used below.

Claim. Let \(N>0\) and \(m\in\mathbb R\), and let \(U\) be \(m\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\). Then \(\bar U_N\) is \(m\)-strongly convex on \(\mathcal Z_N\).

Proof. We first recall why \(V_N\) is \((Nm)\)-strongly convex (). Let \(x,y\in\mathcal Z_N\) and \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). Linearity of \(J_i\) gives \(J_i(ax+by)=aJ_ix+bJ_iy\) and \(J_ix-J_iy=J_i(x-y)\), so (1) for \(U\) at the points \(J_ix\) and \(J_iy\) reads

\[U(J_i(ax+by))\le aU(J_ix)+bU(J_iy)-ab\,\frac m2\,\|J_i(x-y)\|^2.\]

Summing over \(i=1,\dots,N\) and using the norm identity \(\sum_i\|J_i(x-y)\|^2=N\|x-y\|^2\) from the first step,

\[V_N(ax+by)\le aV_N(x)+bV_N(y)-ab\,\frac{Nm}2\,\|x-y\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

Since \(N>0\), the number \(N^{-1}\) is positive, and multiplying (2) by it preserves the inequality. The three function values become values of \(\bar U_N=N^{-1}V_N\), and the last term becomes

\[N^{-1}\cdot ab\,\frac{Nm}2\,\|x-y\|^2=ab\,\frac m2\,\|x-y\|^2,\]

because \(N^{-1}N=1\). The result is (1) for \(f=\bar U_N\). \(\square\)

No sign condition on \(m\) and no relation between \(d_\theta\) and \(d_x\) is needed. The factor \(N\) gained by adding \(N\) copies of \(U\) is removed exactly by the average, so the strong convexity constant of \(\bar U_N\) does not depend on the number of particles, although the dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\) of \(\mathcal Z_N\) does.

steps.title: The averaged parameter force and the unaveraged latent force
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be differentiable, let \(z\in\mathcal Z_N\) with parameter block \(\theta\), and write \(\partial_{\theta_j}U\) and \(\partial_{x_j}U\) for the coordinates of \(\nabla U\) in its parameter and latent blocks. Then for every parameter coordinate \(j\in\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\),

\[F_N(z)_{\theta,j}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i).\qquad(1)\]

If in addition \(N>0\), then for every particle \(i\in\{1,\dots,N\}\) and latent coordinate \(j\in\{1,\dots,d_x\}\),

\[\sqrt N\,F_N(z)_{(i,j)}=\partial_{x_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i).\qquad(2)\]

Proof. We first compute the coordinates of \(\nabla V_N(z)\) (, ). By the chain rule, as in the previous step,

\[DV_N(z)[w]=\sum_{q=1}^NDU(J_qz)[J_qw]=\sum_{q=1}^N\langle\nabla U(J_qz),J_qw\rangle.\]

Let \(e_a\) be the standard basis vector of coordinate \(a\). A parameter basis vector is copied by every \(J_q\): \(J_qe_{\theta,j}=e_{\theta,j}\). A latent basis vector \(e_{(i,j)}\) is seen only by particle \(i\): \(J_qe_{(i,j)}=\sqrt N\,e_{x,j}\) if \(q=i\) and \(J_qe_{(i,j)}=0\) if \(q\ne i\). Since \(\partial_aV_N(z)=DV_N(z)[e_a]\), we obtain

\[\partial_{\theta_j}V_N(z)=\sum_{q=1}^N\partial_{\theta_j}U(J_qz),\qquad\partial_{(i,j)}V_N(z)=\sqrt N\,\partial_{x_j}U(J_iz).\]

The coordinates of the scalar multiple \(F_N=N^{-1}\nabla V_N\) are \(N^{-1}\) times those of \(\nabla V_N\). The first identity therefore gives (1), because \(J_qz=(\theta,\sqrt Nz_q)\). For (2), multiply the second identity by \(N^{-1}\) and then by \(\sqrt N\):

\[\sqrt N\,F_N(z)_{(i,j)}=\sqrt N\cdot N^{-1}\cdot\sqrt N\,\partial_{x_j}U(J_iz)=\bigl((\sqrt N)^2N^{-1}\bigr)\,\partial_{x_j}U(J_iz)=\partial_{x_j}U(J_iz),\]

since \((\sqrt N)^2=N\) for \(N\ge0\) and \(NN^{-1}=1\) for \(N\ne0\). \(\square\)

In physical coordinates \(X^i=\sqrt Nz_i\), identity (1) says that the parameter force is the average \(N^{-1}\sum_i\nabla_\theta U(\theta,X^i)\), and identity (2) says that the latent force, once the scaling is undone, is the single-particle gradient \(\nabla_xU(\theta,X^i)\). The parameter occurs in every summand of \(V_N\), whereas the latent block of particle \(i\) occurs only in the \(i\)th summand; this is the origin of the different normalizations of the parameter and latent equations in the particle algorithms.

steps.title: The force has the Lipschitz constant of the pair gradient
steps.body:
Lipschitz maps. For \(L\ge0\), a map \(G\) between normed spaces is \(L\)-Lipschitz if \(\|G(x)-G(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\).

Claim. Let \(N>0\) and \(L\ge0\), let \(U\) be differentiable, and let \(\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\). Then \(F_N\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathcal Z_N\).

Proof. We first show that \(\nabla V_N\) is \(NL\)-Lipschitz (). Let \(x,y,w\in\mathcal Z_N\) and put \(g=\nabla V_N(x)-\nabla V_N(y)\). The chain-rule formula of the previous step, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), the Lipschitz property of \(\nabla U\) and linearity of \(J_i\) give

\[\langle g,w\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl\langle\nabla U(J_ix)-\nabla U(J_iy),J_iw\bigr\rangle\le L\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_i(x-y)\|\,\|J_iw\|.\]

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for finite sums, \(\sum_ia_ib_i\le(\sum_ia_i^2)^{1/2}(\sum_ib_i^2)^{1/2}\), together with the norm identity \(\sum_i\|J_iu\|^2=N\|u\|^2\) from the first step, gives

\[\sum_{i=1}^N\|J_i(x-y)\|\,\|J_iw\|\le\bigl(N\|x-y\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(N\|w\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}=N\|x-y\|\,\|w\|.\]

Taking \(w=g\) yields \(\|g\|^2\le NL\|x-y\|\,\|g\|\). If \(g=0\), the bound \(\|g\|\le NL\|x-y\|\) holds trivially; otherwise divide by \(\|g\|>0\). Hence

\[\|\nabla V_N(x)-\nabla V_N(y)\|\le NL\|x-y\|.\qquad(1)\]

Now \(F_N(x)-F_N(y)=N^{-1}g\) with \(N^{-1}>0\). By homogeneity of the norm and (1),

\[\|F_N(x)-F_N(y)\|=N^{-1}\|g\|\le N^{-1}\cdot NL\|x-y\|=L\|x-y\|.\qquad\square\]

Combined with the previous steps, \(F_N=\nabla\bar U_N\), where \(\bar U_N\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. The theory of kinetic Langevin dynamics for one strongly convex potential with Lipschitz gradient therefore applies to the particle system with the constants \(m\) and \(L\) of the pair potential; only the dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\) of the state space depends on \(N\).

KIPLMC/Exponential.lean.title: The KIPLMC1 exponential update in parameter and latent coordinates
KIPLMC/Exponential.lean.summary:
KIPLMC1 is the exponential integrator of Dalalyan and Riou-Durand applied to the kinetic particle system. A phase state is a pair \((v,z)\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), velocity first, where \(\mathcal Z_N=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times(\mathbb R^{d_x})^N\) is the scaled particle space of the previous section. With the response functions \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\), \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k(s)\,ds\), the force \(F_N\) and the amplitude \(a_N=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\), one step of step size \(h\) with innovation \((\xi,\xi')\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) is

\[v^+=\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F_N(z)+a_N\xi,\qquad z^+=z+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F_N(z)+a_N\xi'.\]

This section defines this update and the sequence it generates from a given innovation sequence, and proves that in coordinates it is Algorithm 1 of the paper: the parameter coordinates contain the averaged parameter gradient with noise amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\), and after multiplication by \(\sqrt N\) the latent coordinates contain the single-particle gradient with noise amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\). The innovation is arbitrary here; its correlated Gaussian law is constructed in a later section, and the probability laws of the resulting chain are studied after that.

steps.title: The response functions and the particle exponential update
steps.body:
Definition. Fix \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\). The response functions are \(\psi_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\) and \(\psi_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi_k(s)\,ds\) for \(k\ge0\) and \(t\in\mathbb R\). For \(\gamma\ne0\),

\[\psi_1(t)=\frac{1-e^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma},\qquad\psi_2(t)=\frac{t-\psi_1(t)}{\gamma},\]

and for \(\gamma=0\) one has \(\psi_1(t)=t\), \(\psi_2(t)=t^2/2\). For a map \(G:\mathcal Z_N\to\mathcal Z_N\), a step size \(h\in\mathbb R\), a phase state \((v,z)\) and an innovation \((\xi,\xi')\), the exponential update is

\[\Phi_{G,\gamma,h}\bigl((v,z),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=\bigl(\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)G(z)+\xi,\;z+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)G(z)+\xi'\bigr).\]

The kinetic amplitude is \(a_N=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\), where \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is the real square root, extended by \(\sqrt a=0\) for \(a<0\), and \(N^{-1}=0\) for \(N=0\). The KIPLMC1 update is

\[K\bigl((v,z),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=\Phi_{F_N,\gamma,h}\bigl((v,z),(a_N\xi,a_N\xi')\bigr).\]

Derivation of the deterministic part. The coefficients are those of the exact solution of the kinetic equation with the force frozen at its initial value. Let \(g\in\mathcal Z_N\) be fixed and put \(v(t)=\psi_0(t)v-\psi_1(t)g\), \(x(t)=z+\psi_1(t)v-\psi_2(t)g\). By the fundamental theorem of calculus \(\psi_{k+1}'=\psi_k\), and \(\psi_0'=-\gamma\psi_0\). Integrating the latter from \(0\) to \(t\) gives \(\gamma\psi_1(t)=1-\psi_0(t)\). Hence

\[v'(t)=-\gamma\psi_0(t)v-\psi_0(t)g=-\gamma\bigl(\psi_0(t)v-\psi_1(t)g\bigr)-\bigl(\gamma\psi_1(t)+\psi_0(t)\bigr)g=-\gamma v(t)-g,\]

and \(x'(t)=\psi_0(t)v-\psi_1(t)g=v(t)\), with \(v(0)=v\), \(x(0)=z\) because \(\psi_0(0)=1\) and \(\psi_1(0)=\psi_2(0)=0\) (, ). Thus the deterministic part of \(\Phi_{G,\gamma,h}\) is the time-\(h\) solution of \(v'=-\gamma v-g\), \(x'=v\) with \(g=G(z)\). For the stochastic equation \(dv=(-\gamma v-g)\,dt+a_N\,dB\) the variation of constants formula adds the Wiener integrals \(a_N\int_0^h\psi_0(h-s)\,dB_s\) to the velocity and \(a_N\int_0^h\psi_1(h-s)\,dB_s\) to the position; these are the components \(a_N\xi\) and \(a_N\xi'\) of the innovation.

The amplitude \(a_N\) corresponds to temperature \(1/N\) in the scaled coordinates: for \(\gamma>0\) the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation \(dv=-\gamma v\,dt+a_N\,dB\) for a single coordinate has stationary variance \(a_N^2/(2\gamma)=1/N\). The definition accepts an arbitrary innovation; for the algorithm, each coordinate pair \((\xi_a,\xi'_a)\) is a centered Gaussian vector with the covariance of the two Wiener integrals above, independently over coordinates and over steps.

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be differentiable, let \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\) and \(N\ge0\), let \((v,z)\) be a phase state with parameter block \(\theta\) of \(z\), let \((\xi,\xi')\) be an innovation, and let \((v^+,z^+)=K((v,z),(\xi,\xi'))\). Then for every parameter coordinate \(j\in\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\),

\[v^+_{\theta,j}=\psi_0(h)\,v_{\theta,j}-\frac{\psi_1(h)}N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)+a_N\,\xi_{\theta,j},\] \[z^+_{\theta,j}=z_{\theta,j}+\psi_1(h)\,v_{\theta,j}-\frac{\psi_2(h)}N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_{\theta_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)+a_N\,\xi'_{\theta,j}.\]

\[v^+_{\theta,j}=\psi_0(h)v_{\theta,j}-\psi_1(h)F_N(z)_{\theta,j}+a_N\xi_{\theta,j},\qquad z^+_{\theta,j}=z_{\theta,j}+\psi_1(h)v_{\theta,j}-\psi_2(h)F_N(z)_{\theta,j}+a_N\xi'_{\theta,j}.\]

By the formula for the parameter coordinates of the force proved in the previous section (), \(F_N(z)_{\theta,j}=N^{-1}\sum_i\partial_{\theta_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\). Substituting and writing \(\psi_k(h)\cdot N^{-1}=\psi_k(h)/N\) for \(k=1,2\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The parameter coordinates are not rescaled, so with \(\theta_n=z_\theta\), \(V^\theta_n=v_\theta\), \(\varepsilon^0_n=\xi_\theta\), \(\varepsilon^{0\prime}_n=\xi'_\theta\) and \(X^i_n=\sqrt Nz_i\) these are the parameter lines of Algorithm 1: the force is the particle average \(F^\theta_n\), and both noises carry the amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). The velocity and position innovations \(\xi_{\theta,j}\) and \(\xi'_{\theta,j}\) are different random variables; for the algorithm they are correlated, since both are integrals of the same Brownian increment.

Claim. Let \(N>0\) and \(\gamma\in\mathbb R\). Then

\[\sqrt N\,a_N=\sqrt N\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}N}=\sqrt{2\gamma}.\qquad(1)\]

If moreover \(U\) is differentiable, \(h\in\mathbb R\), and \((v^+,z^+)=K((v,z),(\xi,\xi'))\), then for every particle \(i\) and latent coordinate \(j\in\{1,\dots,d_x\}\),

\[\sqrt N\,v^+_{(i,j)}=\psi_0(h)\bigl(\sqrt N\,v_{(i,j)}\bigr)-\psi_1(h)\,\partial_{x_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_{(i,j)},\qquad(2)\] \[\sqrt N\,z^+_{(i,j)}=\sqrt N\,z_{(i,j)}+\psi_1(h)\bigl(\sqrt N\,v_{(i,j)}\bigr)-\psi_2(h)\,\partial_{x_j}U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)+\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi'_{(i,j)}.\qquad(3)\]

\[\sqrt N\,v^+_{(i,j)}=\psi_0(h)\sqrt N\,v_{(i,j)}-\psi_1(h)\bigl(\sqrt N\,F_N(z)_{(i,j)}\bigr)+\bigl(\sqrt N\,a_N\bigr)\xi_{(i,j)},\]

The position coordinate is treated in the same way, with \(\psi_1(h)v\) and \(\psi_2(h)F_N(z)\) in place of \(\psi_0(h)v\) and \(\psi_1(h)F_N(z)\), which gives (3). \(\square\)

steps.body:
Definition. Given an initial phase state \(Y_0\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) and an innovation sequence \((\zeta_n)_{n\ge0}\) in \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), the KIPLMC1 sequence is defined by recursion:

\[Y_0\text{ given},\qquad Y_{n+1}=K(Y_n,\zeta_n)\qquad(n\ge0).\]

By the recursion theorem for the natural numbers this defines \(Y_n\) uniquely for every \(n\), for every choice of \(Y_0\) and \((\zeta_n)\); the innovation \(\zeta_n\) is used to produce \(Y_{n+1}\). Writing \(Y_n=(v_n,z_n)\), the previous two steps express \((v_{n+1},z_{n+1})\) in the coordinates \(\theta_n\), \(X^i_n=\sqrt Nz_{n,i}\), \(V^\theta_n\), \(V^{x_i}_n=\sqrt Nv_{n,i}\) of Algorithm 1.

No probabilistic assumption enters the definition: \(Y_n\) is a deterministic function of \(Y_0,\zeta_0,\dots,\zeta_{n-1}\). The algorithm is obtained by taking \(Y_0\) random and \((\zeta_n)\) independent of \(Y_0\), independent across \(n\), each with the correlated Gaussian law of the innovation; the law of \(Y_n\) is then determined in the section on chain laws, and its distance to the target is bounded in the section on the KIPLMC1 error bound.

KIPLMC/Splitting.lean.title: The KIPLMC2 thermostat–kick–drift–kick–thermostat update
KIPLMC/Splitting.lean.summary:
KIPLMC2 is the OBABO splitting scheme applied to the kinetic particle system in the scaled coordinates \(\mathcal Z_N\) of the geometry section. For a step size \(h\), friction \(\gamma\) and a phase state \((v,z)\), velocity first, one step composes five maps: an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half-step (O) on the velocity, a half kick (B) by the force \(F_N\), a full drift (A) of the position, a second half kick at the new position, and a second Ornstein–Uhlenbeck half-step with a fresh noise vector. With \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and \(\sigma_N=\sqrt{(1-\delta^2)/N}\), the result is

\[v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma_N\xi-\tfrac h2F_N(z),\qquad z^+=z+hv_{1/2},\qquad v^+=\delta\bigl(v_{1/2}-\tfrac h2F_N(z^+)\bigr)+\sigma_N\xi'.\]

This section defines the step and proves these formulas, and then proves that in coordinates they are Algorithm 2 of the paper: the parameter half kick uses the averaged parameter gradient, and after multiplication by \(\sqrt N\) the latent half velocity has the unit-temperature thermostat noise \(\sqrt{1-\delta^2}\,\xi\) and the single-particle gradient. All statements are identities for given noise vectors \(\xi,\xi'\); the law of the resulting chain and its convergence are studied in later sections.

steps.title: The five substeps and the KIPLMC2 update
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(E\) be a real vector space, \(G:E\to E\) a map, and \(\delta,\sigma,\tau\in\mathbb R\). On phase states \((v,x)\in E\times E\) define

\[O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi}(v,x)=(\delta v+\sigma\xi,\;x),\qquad B_\tau(v,x)=(v-\tau G(x),\;x),\qquad A_\tau(v,x)=(v,\;x+\tau v),\]

for a noise vector \(\xi\in E\). The OBABO step with step size \(h\) and noise vectors \(\xi,\xi'\) is the composition

\[\mathrm{OBABO}\bigl((v,x),\xi,\xi'\bigr)=O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi'}\circ B_{h/2}\circ A_h\circ B_{h/2}\circ O_{\delta,\sigma,\xi}\,(v,x).\]

For KIPLMC2 take \(E=\mathcal Z_N\), \(G=F_N\), \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\) and

\[\sigma_N=\sqrt{\frac{1-\delta^2}N}=\sqrt{\frac{1-e^{-\gamma h}}N},\]

with the conventions \(\sqrt a=0\) for \(a<0\) and \(N^{-1}=0\) for \(N=0\). The KIPLMC2 step is \(S((v,z),\xi,\xi')=\mathrm{OBABO}((v,z),\xi,\xi')\), and the half velocity is \(v_{1/2}=\delta v+\sigma_N\xi-\frac h2F_N(z)\).

Claim. For all \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\), all phase states \((v,z)\) and all \(\xi,\xi'\in\mathcal Z_N\), the step \(S((v,z),\xi,\xi')=(v^+,z^+)\) satisfies

\[z^+=z+h\,v_{1/2},\qquad v^+=\delta\Bigl(v_{1/2}-\frac h2F_N\bigl(z+h\,v_{1/2}\bigr)\Bigr)+\sigma_N\xi'.\]

Proof. Evaluate the five maps in order. The first thermostat gives \((\delta v+\sigma_N\xi,\,z)\). The half kick subtracts \(\frac h2F_N(z)\) from the velocity, giving \((v_{1/2},\,z)\). The drift gives \((v_{1/2},\,z+hv_{1/2})\); call this position \(z^+\). The second half kick evaluates the force at the current position \(z^+\), giving \((v_{1/2}-\frac h2F_N(z^+),\,z^+)\). The last thermostat multiplies the velocity by \(\delta\) and adds \(\sigma_N\xi'\), and leaves the position unchanged. \(\square\)

The thermostat coefficients. For \(\gamma>0\), the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation \(dv=-\gamma v\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,dB\) solved exactly over a time \(h/2\) gives \(v\mapsto e^{-\gamma h/2}v+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\int_0^{h/2}e^{-\gamma(h/2-s)}\,dB_s\). By the Itô isometry the Wiener integral is centered Gaussian with variance per coordinate

\[\frac{2\gamma}N\int_0^{h/2}e^{-2\gamma(h/2-s)}\,ds=\frac{1-e^{-\gamma h}}N=\sigma_N^2.\]

Hence the O half-step is the exact Ornstein–Uhlenbeck transition when \(\xi\) is a standard Gaussian vector independent of \((v,z)\), and it leaves the Gaussian law with covariance \(N^{-1}I\) invariant, since \(\delta^2N^{-1}+\sigma_N^2=N^{-1}\). The B and A maps are the exact flows of \(v'=-G(x)\) and \(x'=v\) over the indicated times.

The order of the substeps matters: the drift uses the refreshed and kicked half velocity, the second kick uses the force at the new position \(z^+\), and the last thermostat uses a second noise vector \(\xi'\). Only first derivatives of \(U\) enter, through \(F_N\).

KIPLMC/Target.lean.title: The particle Gibbs phase measure and sharp parameter concentration
KIPLMC/Target.lean.summary:
This section constructs the probability measure that the kinetic particle dynamics leaves invariant and computes its parameter marginal. In the scaled coordinates \(\mathcal Z_N\) the velocity part is the Gaussian law \(\kappa_N=\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\), obtained from the standard Gaussian measure by the map \(v\mapsto N^{-1/2}v\). The position part is the lifted Gibbs measure \(\pi_N(dz)=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\) with \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)\). The phase target is the product \(\Pi_N=\kappa_N\otimes\pi_N\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), velocity first.

We prove that \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure, that its position marginal is \(\pi_N\), and that its parameter marginal is the powered likelihood \(\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\propto\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta\), where \(\ell(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\) is the marginal likelihood \(p_\theta(y)\) when \(U=-\log p_\theta(\cdot,y)\). Under \(m\)-strong convexity of \(U\) with \(m>0\), the marginal likelihood has a unique maximizer \(\theta_\star\) (the maximum marginal likelihood estimator), and

\[\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2\,\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\le\frac{d_\theta}{Nm}.\]

This is Proposition 2 of the paper with its sharp constant, and the term \(\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\) appears in every parameter error bound of the report. Invariance of \(\Pi_N\) under the dynamics is a separate statement, proved in the section on stationarity.

steps.title: The thermal velocity law
steps.body:
Definitions. For a measure \(\mu\) on a space \(A\) and a measurable map \(f:A\to B\), the pushforward \(f_\#\mu\) is the measure \(f_\#\mu(S)=\mu(f^{-1}(S))\) on measurable sets \(S\subseteq B\); if \(X\) has law \(\mu\), then \(f(X)\) has law \(f_\#\mu\). The standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\) on the Euclidean space \(\mathcal Z_N\) is the law of a random vector whose coordinates in an orthonormal basis are independent standard normal variables; it has density \((2\pi)^{-D/2}e^{-\|v\|^2/2}\) with \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). The thermal velocity law is

\[\kappa_N=(s_N)_\#\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N},\qquad s_N(v)=N^{-1/2}v,\]

with the convention \(N^{-1/2}=0\) for \(N=0\). For \(N>0\), \(\kappa_N\) is the centered Gaussian law \(\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\): if \(G\sim\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\), then \(N^{-1/2}G\) has independent centered normal coordinates with variance \(1/N\).

Claim. For every \(N\ge0\), \(\kappa_N\) is a probability measure.

Proof. The map \(s_N\) is linear, hence continuous and Borel measurable. Since \(s_N^{-1}(\mathcal Z_N)=\mathcal Z_N\), we get \(\kappa_N(\mathcal Z_N)=\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}(\mathcal Z_N)=1\). \(\square\)

The variance \(1/N\) per coordinate is the temperature of the scaled velocities: undoing the scaling, the parameter velocity has covariance \(N^{-1}I_{d_\theta}\) and each physical latent velocity \(\sqrt N v_i\) has covariance \(I_{d_x}\), which are the initial velocity laws in the paper's theorems.

steps.title: The phase target and its position marginal
steps.body:
Definitions. The lifted Gibbs measure is \(\pi_N(dz)=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\), where \(dz\) is Lebesgue measure and \(Z_N=\int_{\mathcal Z_N}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz\in(0,\infty]\). The phase target is the product measure

\[\Pi_N=\kappa_N\otimes\pi_N\quad\text{on }\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N,\qquad\Pi_N(A\times B)=\kappa_N(A)\,\pi_N(B),\]

with the velocity in the first factor. For \(N>0\) it has density proportional to \(\exp(-V_N(z)-\frac N2\|v\|^2)\).

Claim. Let \(N>0\) and \(m>0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(\Pi_N\) is a probability measure, and its position marginal is \(\pi_N\): if \(p(v,z)=z\), then \(p_\#\Pi_N=\pi_N\).

Proof. First, \(\pi_N\) is a probability measure (). Indeed, \(V_N\) is differentiable and \((Nm)\)-strongly convex (geometry section), and strong convexity gives the quadratic lower bound \(V_N(z)\ge V_N(0)+\langle\nabla V_N(0),z\rangle+\frac{Nm}2\|z\|^2\). Hence \(e^{-V_N}\) is bounded by a multiple of a Gaussian density, so \(Z_N<\infty\); and \(Z_N>0\) because the integrand is strictly positive. Dividing by \(Z_N\) gives total mass \(1\).

By the defining property of the product measure, \(\Pi_N(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N)=\kappa_N(\mathcal Z_N)\,\pi_N(\mathcal Z_N)=1\cdot1=1\). For a measurable \(B\subseteq\mathcal Z_N\),

\[p_\#\Pi_N(B)=\Pi_N(\mathcal Z_N\times B)=\kappa_N(\mathcal Z_N)\,\pi_N(B)=\pi_N(B),\]

because \(p^{-1}(B)=\mathcal Z_N\times B\) and \(\kappa_N\) has total mass \(1\) by the previous step. \(\square\)

The velocity and the position are independent under \(\Pi_N\). The position marginal is exactly the normalized lifted Gibbs measure of the particle method; no unnormalized densities need to be compared.

steps.title: The parameter marginal is the powered likelihood
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(\ell(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty]\) be the marginal density of the parameter; for \(U(\theta,x)=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\) it is the marginal likelihood \(p_\theta(y)\). The powered marginal target is

\[\pi_\Theta(d\theta)=\frac{\ell(\theta)^N}{\int\ell(\vartheta)^N\,d\vartheta}\,d\theta\qquad\text{on }\mathbb R^{d_\theta}.\]

Let \(P_\theta:\mathcal Z_N\to\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) be the projection onto the parameter block.

Claim. Let \(N>0\), \(m>0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then the image of \(\Pi_N\) under \((v,z)\mapsto P_\theta z\) is \(\pi_\Theta\).

Proof. The map \((v,z)\mapsto P_\theta z\) is the composition of \(p(v,z)=z\) and \(P_\theta\), both continuous and therefore measurable. For measurable maps the pushforward of a composition is the composition of pushforwards, \((P_\theta\circ p)_\#\Pi_N=(P_\theta)_\#(p_\#\Pi_N)\), since both sides assign the mass \(\Pi_N(p^{-1}(P_\theta^{-1}(S)))\) to a measurable set \(S\). By the previous step \(p_\#\Pi_N=\pi_N\). It remains to compute \((P_\theta)_\#\pi_N\) (). For a Borel set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\), Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative integrand \(e^{-V_N}=\prod_ie^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)}\) gives

\[\int_{\{P_\theta z\in S\}}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz=\int_S\prod_{i=1}^N\Bigl(\int_{\mathbb R^{d_x}}e^{-U(\theta,\sqrt Nz_i)}\,dz_i\Bigr)d\theta=N^{-Nd_x/2}\int_S\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta,\]

where the change of variables \(x=\sqrt Nz_i\), \(dz_i=N^{-d_x/2}dx\), was made in each inner integral. Taking \(S=\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) gives \(Z_N=N^{-Nd_x/2}\int\ell^N\), and since \(0<Z_N<\infty\) the factor \(N^{-Nd_x/2}\) cancels in the quotient:

\[\pi_N(P_\theta z\in S)=\frac{\int_S\ell(\theta)^N\,d\theta}{\int\ell(\vartheta)^N\,d\vartheta}=\pi_\Theta(S).\qquad\square\]

Thus the stationary parameter law has density proportional to \(p_\theta(y)^N=e^{-N\kappa(\theta)}\) with \(\kappa=-\log p_\theta(y)\), which is Proposition 1 of the paper. Raising \(\ell\) to the power \(N\) does not move its maximizer, but concentrates the law around it as \(N\) grows; the particle number acts as an inverse temperature.

steps.title: The unique marginal maximizer and the sharp second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex.

  1. There is exactly one \(\theta_\star\in\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(\ell(\vartheta)\le\ell(\theta_\star)\) for all \(\vartheta\); it is called the marginal maximizer.
  2. If \(N>0\) and \(\theta_\star\) is a marginal maximizer, then \(\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2\,\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\le\dfrac{d_\theta}{Nm}\).
  3. Under the same hypotheses, \(\Bigl(\int_{\mathcal Z_N}\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2\,\pi_N(dz)\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{\dfrac{d_\theta}{Nm}}\); in particular this second moment is finite.

Proof. Strong convexity of \(U\) makes \(0<\ell(\theta)<\infty\) for every \(\theta\), so \(\kappa=-\log\ell\) is real valued; it is continuous, and by the Prékopa–Leindler inequality it is \(m\)-strongly convex (). Since \(-\log\) is strictly decreasing on \((0,\infty)\), \(\theta_\star\) maximizes \(\ell\) if and only if it minimizes \(\kappa\).

Part 1. A continuous \(m\)-strongly convex function on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\) with \(m>0\) grows at least quadratically, so it attains its minimum, and it is strictly convex, so the minimizer is unique ().

Part 2. Put \(F=N\kappa\), which is continuous, \(q\)-strongly convex with \(q=Nm>0\), and minimized at \(\theta_\star\); then \(\pi_\Theta\) has density \(e^{-F}/\int e^{-F}\), because \(\ell^N=e^{-F}\). We use the sharp concentration theorem for such Gibbs measures (), whose proof is the following dilation argument. Write \(d=d_\theta\), \(\theta=\theta_\star+w\). Applying strong convexity at the points \(\theta_\star\) and \(\theta_\star+w\) with weights \(1-t,t\) and using \(F(\theta_\star)\le F(\theta_\star+tw)\), dividing by \(t\) and letting \(t\to0\), gives the growth bound \(F(\theta_\star)\le F(\theta_\star+w)-\frac q2\|w\|^2\). For \(0<r<1\), strong convexity with weights \(r,1-r\) and this growth bound give

\[F(\theta_\star+rw)\le rF(\theta_\star+w)+(1-r)F(\theta_\star)-r(1-r)\tfrac q2\|w\|^2\le F(\theta_\star+w)-\tfrac q2(1-r^2)\|w\|^2.\]

Exponentiating, using \(e^s\ge1+s\), integrating in \(w\), and changing variables \(w'=rw\) on the left (Jacobian \(r^{-d}\)) yields, with \(Z=\int e^{-F}\) and \(M=\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2e^{-F(\theta)}\,d\theta\),

\[r^{-d}Z\ge Z+\tfrac q2(1-r^2)M,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad\frac{r^{-d}-1}{1-r}\,Z\ge\tfrac q2(1+r)M.\]

As \(r\to1\), the left side tends to \(dZ\) (the derivative of \(r\mapsto r^{-d}\) at \(1\) is \(-d\)) and the right side to \(qM\). Hence \(M/Z\le d/q=d_\theta/(Nm)\), which is part 2 ().

Part 3. By the previous step \((P_\theta)_\#\pi_N=\pi_\Theta\), so the change of variables formula for pushforwards gives \(\int\|P_\theta z-\theta_\star\|^2\,\pi_N(dz)=\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2\,\pi_\Theta(d\theta)\), and part 2 and monotonicity of the square root give part 3 (). \(\square\)

The constant is sharp: if \(F\) is the quadratic \(\frac q2\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2\), then \(\pi_\Theta=\mathcal N(\theta_\star,q^{-1}I)\) and equality holds. Since the only coupling of a law with a point mass is the product coupling, the quantity in part 3 is the Wasserstein distance \(W_2(\pi_\Theta,\delta_{\theta_\star})\), so part 3 is Proposition 2 of the paper. The bound is about the spread around the maximizer, not around the mean of \(\pi_\Theta\).

KIPLMC/Dynamics.lean.title: Physical-time particle integral solutions and synchronous contraction
KIPLMC/Dynamics.lean.summary:
In the scaled coordinates \(\mathcal Z_N\) of the geometry section, the kinetic interacting particle Langevin diffusion (KIPLD) of the paper reads

\[dz_t=v_t\,dt,\qquad dv_t=\bigl(-\gamma v_t-F_N(z_t)\bigr)\,dt+\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,dW_t,\]

where \(W\) is a standard Brownian motion on \(\mathcal Z_N\), \(z=(\theta,X^1/\sqrt N,\dots,X^N/\sqrt N)\) and \(v=(V^\theta,V^{x_1}/\sqrt N,\dots,V^{x_N}/\sqrt N)\). By the coordinate formulas for \(F_N\), the parameter and latent components of this equation are exactly the equations (KIPLD) of the paper, in physical time.

Because \(F_N=\nabla\bar U_N\) with \(\bar U_N\) \(m\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, the kinetic theory for a single potential applies with the original constants. This section records the two analytic consequences used later: the integral form of the equation has a continuous solution on every finite time interval for every continuous additive input, and two solutions driven by the same input and started with the same velocity approach each other at the rate \(e^{-mt/\gamma}\), whenever \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\). Neither the dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\) nor the temperature \(1/N\) enters this rate. These are statements about paths; laws and stationarity are treated in later sections.

steps.title: Differentiability and smoothness of the averaged potential
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U\) be differentiable. Then \( ar U_N\) is differentiable for every \(N\ge0\). If moreover \(N>0\), \(L\ge0\) and \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then \( abla ar U_N\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Proof. The lifted potential \(V_N=\sum_iU\circ J_i\) is differentiable as a finite sum of compositions of a differentiable function with linear maps (), and a constant multiple of a differentiable function is differentiable; hence \( ar U_N=N^{-1}V_N\) is differentiable. By the gradient identity of the geometry section, \( abla ar U_N(z)=F_N(z)\) for every \(z\) (), so the maps \( abla ar U_N\) and \(F_N\) coincide. Under the additional hypotheses \(F_N\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz (), hence so is \( abla ar U_N\). \(\square\)

Together with the strong convexity of \( ar U_N\) proved in the geometry section, \( ar U_N\) satisfies the three hypotheses of the kinetic contraction theory for a potential \(f\): differentiability, \(m\)-strong convexity, and an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, with the constants of \(U\).

steps.title: Integral solutions of the particle equation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N>0\), let \(L,\gamma\ge0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let \((v_0,z_0)\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), let \(B:\mathbb R\to\mathcal Z_N\) be continuous with \(B(0)=0\), and let \(T\ge0\). Then there is a continuous path \(t\mapsto(v_t,z_t)\) in \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) with \((v_0,z_0)\) at time \(0\) such that for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[v_t-v_0=-\int_0^t\bigl(\gamma v_s+F_N(z_s)\bigr)\,ds+B(t),\qquad z_t-z_0=\int_0^tv_s\,ds.\qquad(1)\]

Equivalently, with \(D(v,z)=(\gamma v+F_N(z),\,-v)\), the phase path \(Y_t=(v_t,z_t)\) satisfies \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tD(Y_s)\,ds+(B(t),0)\). If \(B\) is a path of \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,W\) for a Brownian motion \(W\), then (1) is the integral form of the particle diffusion above; for an arbitrary continuous \(B\) it is a deterministic integral equation.

Proof. The map \(D\) is globally Lipschitz on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\). Indeed, by the triangle inequality and the \(L\)-Lipschitz property of \(F_N\) (),

\[\|\gamma(v-v')+F_N(z)-F_N(z')\|\le\gamma\|v-v'\|+L\|z-z'\|,\qquad\|-v+v'\|=\|v-v'\|,\]

so \(D\) is \((\gamma+L+1)\)-Lipschitz for the norm \(\max(\|v\|,\|z\|)\) on the product. The input \(t\mapsto(B(t),0)\) is continuous and vanishes at \(0\). For a globally Lipschitz drift and a continuous additive input, the integral equation \(Y_t=Y_0-\int_0^tD(Y_s)\,ds+(B(t),0)\) has a continuous solution on \([0,T]\) (). That theorem is proved by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem on intervals of length \(\delta=1/(2(K+1))\), \(K\) the Lipschitz constant, on which the integral operator is a contraction, and by joining the solutions on the consecutive intervals \([k\delta,(k+1)\delta]\) by induction on \(k\) (). Reading the two components of the phase equation gives (1). \(\square\)

The friction coefficient of the equation is \(\gamma\) and the velocity has unit inverse mass, because the force is already the gradient of the averaged potential. The probabilistic content, namely which input \(B\) is used and what the law of the solution is, is added in the sections on the diffusion law and on the Brownian particle flow.

steps.title: The contraction rate does not depend on the particle number
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N>0\), \(m\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\) and \(\gamma>0\) with \(m\le L\) and \(m+L\le\gamma^2\), and let \(U\) be differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let \(T\in\mathbb R\) and let \(v,x,y:\mathbb R\to\mathcal Z_N\) be continuous on \([0,T]\) with \(v(0)=0\), and suppose that for every \(t\in[0,T)\)

\[v'(t)=-\gamma v(t)-\bigl(F_N(x(t))-F_N(y(t))\bigr),\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(x(t)-y(t)\bigr)=v(t).\qquad(1)\]

Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[\|x(t)-y(t)\|\le\sqrt2\,e^{-mt/\gamma}\,\|x(0)-y(0)\|.\]

Meaning of the hypotheses. If \((v^1,x)\) and \((v^2,y)\) solve the integral equation of the previous step with the same input \(B\), then \(v=v^1-v^2\) and \(x-y\) satisfy (1): the input cancels in the difference, and the equation becomes differentiable even though \(B\) need not be. The hypothesis \(v(0)=0\) says that the two solutions start with the same velocity.

Proof. By the previous step and the geometry section, the potential \(f=\bar U_N\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient \(\nabla f=F_N\). Hence (1) is the synchronous difference equation \(v'=-\gamma v-(\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y))\), \((x-y)'=v\) of the kinetic theory for \(f\), and the claim is the position contraction theorem of the kinetic report (). We recall its mechanism. Put \(w=x-y\), \(\Delta=\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\) and \(E=\|v+\gamma w\|^2+\|v\|^2\). Strong convexity and the Lipschitz bound give the interpolation inequality \(mL\|w\|^2+\|\Delta\|^2\le(m+L)\langle\Delta,w\rangle\); combined with \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\) and \(m\le L\), it yields the differential inequality \(E'(t)\le-\frac{2m}\gamma E(t)\), and Grönwall's inequality gives \(E(t)\le e^{-2mt/\gamma}E(0)\). Since \((v+\gamma w)+(-v)=\gamma w\), the inequality \(\|a+b\|^2\le2\|a\|^2+2\|b\|^2\) gives \(\gamma^2\|w(t)\|^2\le2E(t)\), while \(v(0)=0\) gives \(E(0)=\gamma^2\|w(0)\|^2\). Hence

\[\gamma^2\|w(t)\|^2\le2e^{-2mt/\gamma}\gamma^2\|w(0)\|^2,\]

and dividing by \(\gamma^2>0\) and taking square roots proves the claim. \(\square\)

If \(T<0\) the interval \([0,T]\) is empty and the statement is vacuous. The rate \(m/\gamma\) and the constant \(\sqrt2\) are those of the pair potential: neither the number of particles nor the dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\) appears, and the noise amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) has cancelled. The friction condition is the paper's \(\gamma\ge\sqrt{\mu+L}\) with \(\mu=m\).

KIPLMC/Laws.lean.title: Measurable particle transitions and the laws of their recursions
KIPLMC/Laws.lean.summary:
Both particle algorithms are recursions \(Y_{n+1}=\Phi(Y_n,\zeta_n)\) on phase space \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), driven by fresh innovations \(\zeta_n\). This section turns them into Markov chains. For a measurable update \(\Phi\), an innovation law \(\eta\) and an initial law \(\mu\), the laws of the iterates are defined by

\[\mu_0=\mu,\qquad\mu_{n+1}=\Phi_\#(\mu_n\otimes\eta),\]

that is, \(\mu_{n+1}\) is the law of \(\Phi(Y,\zeta)\) when \(Y\sim\mu_n\) and \(\zeta\sim\eta\) are independent. We prove that the KIPLMC1 update \(K\) and the KIPLMC2 update \(S\) are measurable, that the resulting \(\mu_n\) are probability measures, and that every realization of the recursions with an initial state independent of a sequence of independent innovations with law \(\eta\) has exactly the law \(\mu_n\) at step \(n\). For KIPLMC2 the innovation law is the product of two standard Gaussian laws, one for each thermostat half-step; for KIPLMC1 it is the correlated Gaussian law constructed in the section on the innovation measure. These law identities connect the algorithms to the convergence theorems proved later; they contain no quantitative estimate.

steps.title: The thermostat noise law and measurability of both updates
steps.body:
Definition. The KIPLMC2 noise law is \(\eta_2=\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\otimes\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\), the joint law of two independent standard Gaussian vectors \((\xi,\xi')\); here \(\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\) is the standard Gaussian measure on \(\mathcal Z_N\).

Claim. (a) \(\eta_2\) is a probability measure. (b) Let \(N>0\), \(L\ge0\), and let \(U\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. For all \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\), the maps

\[\bigl((v,z),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)\mapsto K\bigl((v,z),(\xi,\xi')\bigr),\qquad\bigl((v,z),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)\mapsto S\bigl((v,z),\xi,\xi'\bigr)\]

from \((\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N)\times(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N)\) to \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) are Borel measurable.

Proof. (a) \(\eta_2(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N)=\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}(\mathcal Z_N)^2=1\).

(b) The force \(F_N\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz (), hence continuous. The KIPLMC1 update is \(\bigl(\psi_0(h)v-\psi_1(h)F_N(z)+a_N\xi,\;z+\psi_1(h)v-\psi_2(h)F_N(z)+a_N\xi'\bigr)\), a combination of the coordinate projections, the continuous map \(F_N\), vector addition and multiplication by fixed scalars, so it is continuous. The KIPLMC2 update is the composition of the five continuous substeps \(O\), \(B\), \(A\), \(B\), \(O\), in which the force appears only through \(F_N(z)\) and \(F_N(z+hv_{1/2})\); it is continuous for the same reason. A continuous map between finite-dimensional normed spaces is measurable for the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras, because preimages of open sets are open. \(\square\)

Measurability is what makes the laws \(\Phi_\#(\mu_n\otimes\eta)\) of the next step meaningful. The Lipschitz hypothesis is used only through the continuity of \(F_N\).

steps.title: Markov transitions and the laws of the iterates
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\Phi:H\times Z\to H\) be measurable, \(\eta\) a probability measure on the innovation space \(Z\) and \(\mu\) a probability measure on \(H\). The Markov laws are \(\mu_0=\mu\) and \(\mu_{n+1}=\Phi_\#(\mu_n\otimes\eta)\). Equivalently, \(\mu_{n+1}=\mu_nP\) for the Markov kernel \(P(y,A)=\eta(\{\zeta:\Phi(y,\zeta)\in A\})\), since by Fubini–Tonelli

\[\Phi_\#(\mu_n\otimes\eta)(A)=\int_H\eta\bigl(\{\zeta:\Phi(y,\zeta)\in A\}\bigr)\,\mu_n(dy).\]

The KIPLMC1 laws \(\mu^{(1)}_n(\mu,\eta)\) are the Markov laws for \(\Phi=K\), with initial phase law \(\mu\) and an innovation law \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) that is left as a parameter. The KIPLMC2 laws \(\mu^{(2)}_n(\mu)\) are the Markov laws for \(\Phi((v,z),(\xi,\xi'))=S((v,z),\xi,\xi')\) with \(\eta=\eta_2\).

Claim. Let \(N>0\), \(L\ge0\), \(U\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\), and \(\mu,\eta\) probability measures. Then \(\mu^{(1)}_n(\mu,\eta)\) and \(\mu^{(2)}_n(\mu)\) are probability measures for every \(n\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\) the law is \(\mu\). If \(\mu_n\) is a probability measure, then so is the product \(\mu_n\otimes\eta\), and the pushforward by the measurable map \(\Phi\) of the previous step has total mass \((\mu_n\otimes\eta)(\Phi^{-1}(H))=(\mu_n\otimes\eta)(H\times Z)=1\). \(\square\)

The innovation law of KIPLMC1 is kept general here so that the correlated Gaussian law can be inserted later; probability of \(\eta\) is the only property used in this step.

steps.title: The correlated Gaussian laws of KIPLMC1
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\eta_1(\gamma,h)\) be the KIPLMC1 innovation law on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) constructed in the section on the innovation measure (): the coordinate pairs \((\xi_a,\xi'_a)\), \(a\in I_N\), are independent, and each is a centered Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^2\) with covariance

\[C(\gamma,h)=\int_0^h\begin{pmatrix}\psi_0(t)^2&\psi_0(t)\psi_1(t)\\\psi_0(t)\psi_1(t)&\psi_1(t)^2\end{pmatrix}dt.\]

The Gaussian KIPLMC1 laws are \(\mu^{(1)}_n(\mu)=\mu^{(1)}_n(\mu,\eta_1(\gamma,h))\).

The update multiplies this innovation by \(a_N=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\). For \(\gamma\ge0\), \(h\ge0\) and a Brownian motion \(W\), the pair \(\bigl(\int_0^h\psi_0(h-s)\,dW_s,\int_0^h\psi_1(h-s)\,dW_s\bigr)\) of Wiener integrals is centered Gaussian with this covariance by the Itô isometry, after the substitution \(t=h-s\); so \(\mu^{(1)}_n(\mu)\) is the law of the exponential integrator driven by the exact stochastic integrals of the frozen-force equation, which is Algorithm 1. The velocity and position innovations are correlated: the off-diagonal entry \(\int_0^h\psi_0\psi_1\,dt\) is positive for \(h>0\). Replacing \(\eta_1\) by a product of two independent Gaussian vectors would define a different algorithm.

steps.title: Every realization of KIPLMC1 has the Markov laws
steps.body:
Definitions. For \(\Phi:H\times Z\to H\), an initial point \(y\) and a sequence \(w=(w_n)\) in \(Z\), the noise-driven recursion is \(Y_0=y\), \(Y_{n+1}=\Phi(Y_n,w_n)\). Random variables \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) are mutually independent if \(\mathbb P(X_{j_1}\in A_1,\dots,X_{j_k}\in A_k)=\prod_r\mathbb P(X_{j_r}\in A_r)\) for all distinct indices and measurable sets; the law of \(X\) is \(\mathbb P_X=X_\#\mathbb P\).

Claim. (a) For every initial state and every innovation sequence, the KIPLMC1 sequence of the exponential section coincides with the noise-driven recursion for \(\Phi=K\).

(b) Let \(N>0\), \(L\ge0\), \(U\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\). Let \(X:\Omega\to\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) and \(W_n:\Omega\to\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) (\(n\ge0\)) be almost everywhere measurable, such that \(X\) is independent of the whole sequence \((W_n)_{n\ge0}\), the \(W_n\) are mutually independent, and every \(W_n\) has law \(\eta\), a probability measure. Let \(Y_n(\omega)\) be the KIPLMC1 sequence started at \(X(\omega)\) with innovations \(W_k(\omega)\). Then \(\mathbb P_{Y_n}=\mu^{(1)}_n(\mathbb P_X,\eta)\) for every \(n\).

Proof. (a) Induction on \(n\): both sequences start at the given state, and both successor values apply \(K\) to the previous value and the \(n\)th innovation.

(b) By (a) it suffices to treat the noise-driven recursion, for which this is the Markov law theorem of the unadjusted Langevin report (), applicable because \(K\) is measurable by the first step. Its proof is an induction on \(n\). The base case is \(\mathbb P_{Y_0}=\mathbb P_X\). For the step, \(Y_n\) is a measurable function of \((X,W_0,\dots,W_{n-1})\). The independence hypotheses imply that \(W_n\) is independent of the vector \((X,W_0,\dots,W_{n-1})\): independence of \(X\) from the whole sequence, together with mutual independence of the \(W_k\), gives mutual independence of \(X,W_0,W_1,\dots\), and disjoint groups of mutually independent variables are independent. Hence \(W_n\) is independent of \(Y_n\), the joint law of \((Y_n,W_n)\) is \(\mathbb P_{Y_n}\otimes\eta\), and

\[\mathbb P_{Y_{n+1}}=K_\#\bigl(\mathbb P_{Y_n}\otimes\eta\bigr)=K_\#\bigl(\mu^{(1)}_n(\mathbb P_X,\eta)\otimes\eta\bigr)=\mu^{(1)}_{n+1}(\mathbb P_X,\eta)\]

by the induction hypothesis. \(\square\)

Independence of the current state from the fresh innovation is derived, not assumed: the hypotheses concern only the initial state and the innovation sequence, as in any execution of Algorithm 1 that draws fresh noise at every step.

Definition. The KIPLMC2 sequence started at \(y\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) with innovation pairs \(w_n=(\xi_n,\xi'_n)\) is the noise-driven recursion

\[Y_0=y,\qquad Y_{n+1}=S(Y_n,\xi_n,\xi'_n).\]

Let \(X\) and \(W_n=(\xi_n,\xi'_n)\) be almost everywhere measurable random variables with values in \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\) such that \(X\) is independent of \((W_n)_{n\ge0}\), the \(W_n\) are mutually independent, and every \(W_n\) has law \(\eta_2=\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\otimes\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\). Two different independence structures are involved. Within a step, the law \(\eta_2\) makes the two thermostat noises \(\xi_n\) and \(\xi'_n\) independent standard Gaussian vectors, as in Algorithm 2. Across steps, the pairs \(W_n\) are independent of each other and of the initial state. Within the update the two noises are not used symmetrically: \(\xi_n\) affects the new position through \(v_{1/2}\), whereas \(\xi'_n\) affects only the new velocity.

KIPLMC/Rescaling.lean.title: Velocity and time rescaling of the exponential update
KIPLMC/Rescaling.lean.summary:
The paper's Appendix B identifies both particle algorithms with standard kinetic algorithms for the sum potential \(V_N\) at friction \(\sqrt N\gamma\) and step size \(h/\sqrt N\). The deterministic part of this identification is a change of variables that multiplies the velocity by a constant \(c\ne0\), keeps the position, and changes the clock by the factor \(c\). For a phase state \((v,x)\) write \(D_c(v,x)=(cv,x)\).

This section proves the corresponding identities for an arbitrary normed space \(E\) and force \(G\): \(D_c\) is invertible with inverse \(D_{c^{-1}}\); the exponential update with friction \(c\gamma\), step \(h/c\) and force \(G\) is conjugate by \(D_c\) to the update with friction \(\gamma\), step \(h\) and force \(c^{-2}G\); the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck damping \(e^{-\gamma h/2}\) depends only on the product \(\gamma h\); and for \(c=\sqrt N\) the force factor \(c^{-2}\) is \(N^{-1}\), which turns \(\nabla V_N\) into the particle force \(F_N\). The laws of the Gaussian innovations under the same change of variables are treated in later sections.

steps.title: Velocity rescaling and its inverse
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(E\) be a real normed space and \(c\in\mathbb R\). The velocity rescaling is \(D_c:E\times E\to E\times E\), \(D_c(v,x)=(cv,x)\).

Claim. If \(c\ne0\), then \(D_{c^{-1}}(D_c(v,x))=(v,x)\) for every \((v,x)\in E\times E\).

Proof. \(D_{c^{-1}}(D_c(v,x))=(c^{-1}(cv),x)=((c^{-1}c)v,x)=(v,x)\), since \(c^{-1}c=1\) for \(c\ne0\). \(\square\)

The map \(D_c\) is linear and leaves the position unchanged. In particular, a statement about the position, or about the parameter block of the position, is the same before and after the rescaling; this is why the law identities of later sections transfer error bounds for the position without loss.

steps.title: Conjugation of the exponential update
steps.body:
Notation. For a friction \(\gamma\) write \(\psi_k^\gamma\) for the response functions \(\psi^\gamma_0(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\), \(\psi^\gamma_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^t\psi^\gamma_k(s)\,ds\), and \(\Phi_{G,\gamma,h}\) for the exponential update of the exponential section.

Claim. Let \(E\) be a real normed space, \(G:E\to E\), and \(c,\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\) with \(c\ne0\). For every phase state \((v,x)\) and innovation \((\xi,\xi')\),

\[\Phi_{G,\,c\gamma,\,h/c}\bigl(D_c(v,x),D_c(\xi,\xi')\bigr)=D_c\Bigl(\Phi_{c^{-2}G,\,\gamma,\,h}\bigl((v,x),(\xi,\xi')\bigr)\Bigr).\]

Proof. First, for every \(k\ge0\),

\[\psi^{c\gamma}_k(h/c)=c^{-k}\psi^\gamma_k(h)\qquad(1)\]

(). By induction on \(k\) one shows \(\psi^{c\gamma}_k(t)=c^{-k}\psi^\gamma_k(ct)\) for all \(t\): for \(k=0\), \(e^{-c\gamma t}=\psi^\gamma_0(ct)\); and if it holds for \(k\), the substitution \(u=cs\), \(ds=c^{-1}du\), gives

\[\psi^{c\gamma}_{k+1}(t)=\int_0^tc^{-k}\psi^\gamma_k(cs)\,ds=c^{-k-1}\int_0^{ct}\psi^\gamma_k(u)\,du=c^{-(k+1)}\psi^\gamma_{k+1}(ct).\]

Taking \(t=h/c\) gives (1). Now compute the left side, using \(D_c(\xi,\xi')=(c\xi,\xi')\) and (1) for \(k=0,1,2\). Its velocity component is

\[\psi^\gamma_0(h)\,cv-c^{-1}\psi^\gamma_1(h)\,G(x)+c\xi=c\Bigl(\psi^\gamma_0(h)v-\psi^\gamma_1(h)\,c^{-2}G(x)+\xi\Bigr),\]

and its position component is

\[x+c^{-1}\psi^\gamma_1(h)\,cv-c^{-2}\psi^\gamma_2(h)\,G(x)+\xi'=x+\psi^\gamma_1(h)v-\psi^\gamma_2(h)\,c^{-2}G(x)+\xi'.\]

These are the velocity component multiplied by \(c\) and the unchanged position component of \(\Phi_{c^{-2}G,\gamma,h}((v,x),(\xi,\xi'))\), which is the right side. \(\square\)

With \(c=\sqrt N\), \(G=\nabla V_N\) and the last step of this section, \(c^{-2}G=F_N\): the standard exponential update for the sum potential at friction \(\sqrt N\gamma\) and step \(h/\sqrt N\), applied to \((\sqrt Nv,z)\), is the rescaled KIPLMC1 update. The velocity innovation is multiplied by \(c\) and the position innovation is not; the corresponding statement for the Gaussian laws requires the covariance computation of a later section, because the two innovations scale with different powers of the clock factor.

Claim. (a) For \(c,\gamma,h\in\mathbb R\) with \(c\ne0\),

\[e^{-(c\gamma)(h/c)/2}=e^{-\gamma h/2}.\]

(b) For every integer \(N\ge0\), \(\bigl((\sqrt N)^2\bigr)^{-1}=N^{-1}\).

Proof. (a) The exponents agree: \((c\gamma)(h/c)=\gamma h\,(c/c)=\gamma h\) because \(c\ne0\). (b) \((\sqrt N)^2=N\) because \(N\ge0\); taking inverses gives the claim, including the case \(N=0\) under the convention \(0^{-1}=0\). \(\square\)

Part (a) shows that the OBABO damping \(\delta=e^{-\gamma h/2}\), and hence the thermostat variance \(1-\delta^2\), are unchanged when the friction is multiplied by \(c\) and the step divided by \(c\). KIPLMC.lean.title: Kinetic interacting particle Langevin Monte Carlo: the results of this report
KIPLMC.lean.summary:
This report treats the kinetic interacting particle Langevin Monte Carlo methods of Valsecchi Oliva and Akyildiz for maximum marginal likelihood estimation. A joint potential \(U(\theta,x)=-\log p_\theta(x,y)\) on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\) is given; the goal is the maximizer \(\theta_\star\) of the marginal likelihood \(\ell(\theta)=\int e^{-U(\theta,x)}\,dx\). The standing assumptions are that \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), that \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and that the number of particles \(N\) is positive. The particle state is written in the scaled coordinates \(z=(\theta,X^1/\sqrt N,\dots,X^N/\sqrt N)\) of dimension \(d_\theta+Nd_x\), in which the force of the kinetic particle diffusion is the gradient of the averaged potential \(\bar U_N\), an \(m\)-strongly convex function with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.

The main results are the following. (1) The phase law \(\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\otimes\pi_N\), with \(\pi_N\propto e^{-N\bar U_N}\), is stationary for the kinetic particle diffusion, and its parameter marginal \(\pi_\Theta\) has density proportional to \(\ell(\theta)^N\) (Proposition 1 of the paper). (2) \(\int\|\theta-\theta_\star\|^2\,d\pi_\Theta\le d_\theta/(Nm)\) (Proposition 2). (3) If \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\), the diffusion started with independent thermal velocities converges to \(\pi_N\) in Wasserstein distance at rate \(\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\), and its parameter marginal satisfies the bound of Proposition 3. (4) For KIPLMC1, under \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\) and \(4\gamma Lh\le m\), the root mean square error of \(\theta_n\) about \(\theta_\star\) is at most \(\sqrt2(1-\frac{3mh}{4\gamma})^nW_2(\nu,\pi_N)+\frac{\sqrt2Lh}m\sqrt{d_\theta/N+d_x}+\sqrt{d_\theta/(Nm)}\) (Theorem 1). (5) For KIPLMC2, under \(\gamma^2\ge4L\) and \(33\gamma^3h\le m\), an analogous bound holds with contraction factor \((1-\frac{mh}{3\gamma})^{n/2}\) and bias of order \(h\sqrt{d_\theta/N+d_x}\); it implies the bound of Theorem 2 of the paper with an explicit constant depending only on \(m\), \(L\), \(\gamma\). (6) Explicit choices of \(N\), \(h\) and \(n\) reach a prescribed accuracy \(\varepsilon\). (7) The Bayesian logistic regression model of the experiments has a Lipschitz gradient and is strictly convex when the covariates span the latent space, but it is not strongly convex without additional regularization.

The sections are ordered as follows: the particle geometry and the two update maps; the Gibbs phase target and the concentration of its parameter marginal; integral solutions and Markov laws; the correlated innovation measure and the law of the diffusion; the clock change that identifies both algorithms with standard kinetic algorithms for the sum potential; the error bounds for KIPLMC1 and KIPLMC2; the Brownian particle diffusion and its stationarity; the accuracy budgets; and the logistic example.

KIPLMC/Check.lean.title: The hypotheses on which the main results rest
KIPLMC/Check.lean.summary:
The principal statements of this report are proved from explicitly stated hypotheses only. For the potential: \(U\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^{d_\theta}\times\mathbb R^{d_x}\), \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), and \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, which forces \(m\le L\) whenever \(d_\theta+d_x>0\) and is assumed explicitly where it is used. For the particle system: \(N\ge1\). For the dynamics and the algorithms: a positive friction \(\gamma\) with \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\) for the diffusion; in addition a positive step size \(h\) with \(4\gamma Lh\le m\) for KIPLMC1; and \(\gamma^2\ge4L\) together with a positive step size satisfying \(33\gamma^3h\le m\) for KIPLMC2. For the initialization: an initial position law with finite second moment, and an initial velocity distributed as \(\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\) in scaled coordinates, independent of the initial position.

All further ingredients are constructed or proved rather than assumed: the Brownian motion driving the diffusion, the solution of the particle equation, the stationarity of the Gibbs phase law, the correlated Gaussian innovations of KIPLMC1 and the independent thermostat noises of KIPLMC2, the Markov laws of both chains, the contraction of the OBABO step, and the finiteness of every Wasserstein distance that is converted to a real number. In particular no discrete invariant law of the OBABO chain and no external bias estimate is presupposed. The Brownian motion is constructed as a centered Gaussian process with the Brownian covariance whose values are continuous in mean square; the arguments use only its finite-dimensional laws and this mean-square continuity, so no modification with continuous sample paths is required.

KIPLMC/Noise.lean.title: Correlated Gaussian velocity and position innovations in particle coordinates
KIPLMC/Noise.lean.summary:
One KIPLMC1 step adds to the velocity and to the position two Wiener integrals of the same Brownian increment, \(\int_0^h\psi_0(h-s)\,dW_s\) and \(\int_0^h\psi_1(h-s)\,dW_s\), coordinate by coordinate. In each coordinate this pair is a centered Gaussian vector in \(\mathbb R^2\) with the Gram covariance

\[C(\gamma,h)_{kl}=\int_0^h\psi_k(t)\psi_l(t)\,dt\qquad(k,l\in\{0,1\}),\]

and different coordinates are independent. This section constructs the corresponding probability measure \(\eta_1(\gamma,h)\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal Z_N\): take independent copies of the two-dimensional Gaussian law \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}=\mathcal N(0,C(\gamma,h))\), one for each coordinate of the scaled particle space, and collect the first entries into a velocity vector and the second entries into a position vector. We prove that the construction gives a probability measure, that the blocks of distinct coordinates are independent, and that the velocity–position pair of each coordinate has law exactly \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\). The factor \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) is applied by the update, not by this measure. The construction works for arbitrary dimensions, including \(d_\theta=0\) or \(d_x=0\).

steps.title: Independent Gaussian blocks indexed by the coordinates
steps.body:
Definitions. The coordinate set of \(\mathcal Z_N\) is \(I_N=\{1,\dots,d_\theta\}\sqcup(\{1,\dots,N\}\times\{1,\dots,d_x\})\). Let \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\) be the centered Gaussian measure on \(\mathbb R^2\) with covariance matrix \(C(\gamma,h)\) above, constructed in the kinetic report (). For \(h\ge0\) the matrix \(C(\gamma,h)\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, since for \(u\in\mathbb R^2\)

\[u^{\mathsf T}C(\gamma,h)u=\int_0^h\bigl(u_0\psi_0(t)+u_1\psi_1(t)\bigr)^2\,dt\ge0,\]

so \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\) is the law of a centered Gaussian vector whose covariances are the entries of \(C(\gamma,h)\). The block measure is the finite product

\[\beta_{\gamma,h}=\bigotimes_{a\in I_N}\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\qquad\text{on }(\mathbb R^2)^{I_N},\]

the joint law of independent random vectors \(\omega_a\in\mathbb R^2\), \(a\in I_N\), each with law \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\).

Claim. \(\beta_{\gamma,h}\) is a probability measure.

Proof. A product of finitely many probability measures is a probability measure: the product measure of the whole space is the product of the total masses, \(\prod_{a\in I_N}1=1\). \(\square\)

The entries of \(C(\gamma,h)\) are the covariances of the two Wiener integrals displayed in the summary, by the Itô isometry and the substitution \(t=h-s\); in particular the off-diagonal entry is positive for \(h>0\), so velocity and position innovations of the same coordinate are correlated.

steps.body:

\[A(\omega)=\bigl((\omega_{a,0})_{a\in I_N},\;(\omega_{a,1})_{a\in I_N}\bigr).\]

steps.title: Independence across coordinates and the law of each pair
steps.body:
Claim. (a) Under \(\beta_{\gamma,h}\) the random vectors \(\omega\mapsto\omega_a\), \(a\in I_N\), are mutually independent. (b) For every coordinate \(a\in I_N\), the image of \(\eta_1(\gamma,h)\) under \((\xi,\xi')\mapsto(\xi_a,\xi'_a)\in\mathbb R^2\) is \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\).

(a) For a product of probability measures \(\bigotimes_a\mu_a\) and measurable sets \(S_a\subseteq\mathbb R^2\), the event \(\{\omega_a\in S_a\text{ for all }a\in J\}\) for a finite set \(J\) of indices is the box \(\prod_{a\in J}S_a\times\prod_{a\notin J}\mathbb R^2\), whose measure is \(\prod_{a\in J}\mu_a(S_a)\cdot1\). This is mutual independence of the coordinate maps.

(b) Let \(\pi_a(\xi,\xi')=(\xi_a,\xi'_a)\). The image of \(\eta_1=A_\#\beta_{\gamma,h}\) under \(\pi_a\) is \((\pi_a\circ A)_\#\beta_{\gamma,h}\), since both maps are measurable. By the definition of \(A\), \(\pi_a(A(\omega))=(\omega_{a,0},\omega_{a,1})=\omega_a\), checked on the two entries. Finally, the image of a product of probability measures under the evaluation \(\omega\mapsto\omega_a\) is the factor \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}\): for measurable \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^2\) the preimage is \(S\times\prod_{b\ne a}\mathbb R^2\), of measure \(\mathcal G_{\gamma,h}(S)\). \(\square\)

Multiplication by \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) in the update, and by \(\sqrt N\) when the latent coordinates are unscaled, produces the amplitudes \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) and \(\sqrt{2\gamma}\) of the paper.

KIPLMC/FlowLaw.lean.title: Wasserstein contraction of the physical-time particle position laws
KIPLMC/FlowLaw.lean.summary:
This section turns the integral equation of the particle dynamics into a statement about probability laws. The randomness is described by a source: an initial velocity \(v_0\) and a continuous input path \(B\) on \([0,T]\), with a joint law \(Q\). Starting from an initial position \(z_0\) drawn from a law \(\mu\) independently of the source, one solves the kinetic integral equation for the force \( abla ar U_N=F_N\) and records the position at time \(t\); the law of this position is denoted \(P^Q_t\mu\). For a Brownian source with amplitude \(\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\) this is the position law of the kinetic particle diffusion, but the results hold for every source law.

We prove that \(P^Q_t\mu\) is a probability measure and that, for \(\gamma>0\) and \(\gamma^2\ge m+L\),

\[W_2 igl(P^Q_t\mu,P^Q_t u igr)\le\sqrt2\,e^{-mt/\gamma}\,W_2(\mu, u)\]

for all initial laws with \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), where \(W_2\) is the Wasserstein distance defined as an infimum over all couplings. The constants are those of the pair potential and do not depend on \(N\). No stationary law is used; the comparison with the Gibbs target is made in the section on the Brownian particle flow.

steps.title: The space of continuous input paths
steps.body:
Definition. For \(T\in\mathbb R\) let \(\mathcal C_T=C([0,T];\mathcal Z_N)\) be the space of continuous paths \(B:[0,T]\to\mathcal Z_N\) with the uniform norm \(\|B\|_\infty=\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|B(t)\|\) (for \(T<0\) the interval is empty and \(\mathcal C_T\) has exactly one element). It carries the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of this norm, generated by the open sets. A source is a pair \((v_0,B)\in\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal C_T\), and a source law is a probability measure \(Q\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\times\mathcal C_T\) with the product of the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras.

With the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, every continuous map from \(\mathcal C_T\), or from a product containing it, into a metric space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra is measurable. The flow maps of the next step are continuous in the source, so they are measurable and the laws below are well defined. Measurability alone imposes no relation between the source and the initial position; that relation is fixed by forming product measures.

steps.title: The position law of the particle equation
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(N>0\), \(L,\gamma\ge0\), let \(U\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(T\ge0\). For an initial position \(z_0\) and a source \((v_0,B)\), let \(Y=\Psi(z_0,v_0,B)\) be the continuous solution of

\[Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tD(Y_s)\,ds+\bigl(\bar B(t),0\bigr),\qquad Y_0=(v_0,z_0),\qquad D(v,z)=\bigl(\gamma v+\nabla\bar U_N(z),\,-v\bigr),\]

on \([0,T]\), where \(\bar B(t)=B(\min(\max(t,0),T))-B(0)\) is the input extended to \(\mathbb R\) by freezing it outside \([0,T]\) and shifted to start at \(0\). Such a solution exists by the existence theorem of the dynamics section, and it is unique because \(D\) is Lipschitz; the kinetic report fixes one solution for each \((z_0,v_0,B)\). For \(t\in\mathbb R\), the position law with initial law \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\) and source law \(Q\) is

\[P^Q_t\mu=\Psi_t{}_\#(\mu\otimes Q),\qquad\Psi_t(z_0,(v_0,B))=\text{position component of }Y_t.\]

Thus the initial position is independent of the initial velocity and of the input, which may be dependent on each other in an arbitrary way through \(Q\).

Claim. If moreover \(t\in[0,T]\) and \(\mu,Q\) are probability measures, then \(P^Q_t\mu\) is a probability measure.

Proof. The solution depends Lipschitz continuously on the initial state and on the input in the uniform norm on \([0,T]\) (Grönwall's inequality for the difference of two integral equations with a Lipschitz drift); in particular \(\Psi_t\) is continuous for \(t\in[0,T]\) and hence measurable (). The product \(\mu\otimes Q\) is a probability measure, and the pushforward of a probability measure by a measurable map has total mass \(1\). \(\square\)

The force here is \(\nabla\bar U_N\), which equals the particle force \(F_N\) by the geometry section; its Lipschitz constant \(L\) is the one proved for \(\nabla\bar U_N\) in the dynamics section. With \(B=\sqrt{2\gamma/N}\,W\) for a Brownian motion \(W\) and an initial velocity independent of \(W\), \(P^Q_t\mu\) is the position law of the scaled particle diffusion at time \(t\).

steps.title: Wasserstein contraction of the position laws
steps.body:
Wasserstein distance. For probability measures \(\mu, u\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\), a coupling is a probability measure \(\pi\) on \(\mathcal Z_N imes\mathcal Z_N\) with marginals \(\mu\) and \( u\), and

\[W_2(\mu, u)=\inf_\pi\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\pi(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty],\]

the infimum over all couplings. The product \(\mu\otimes u\) is always a coupling, so the set of couplings is nonempty.

Claim. Let \(N>0\), \(m\in\mathbb R\), \(L,\gamma\ge0\) with \(m\le L\), \(\gamma>0\) and \(m+L\le\gamma^2\), and let \(U\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let \(T\ge0\), \(t\in[0,T]\), let \(\mu, u\) be probability measures on \(\mathcal Z_N\) with \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), and let \(Q\) be a source law. Then

\[W_2 igl(P^Q_t\mu,P^Q_t u igr)\le\sqrt2\,e^{-mt/\gamma}\,W_2(\mu, u).\]

Proof. This is the law-level kinetic contraction theorem () for the potential \(f= ar U_N\), which is differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient by the geometry and dynamics sections. Its argument is the following. Let \(\pi\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\) with finite cost. On the probability space \( igl((\mathcal Z_N imes\mathcal Z_N) imes(\mathcal Z_N imes\mathcal C_T),\pi\otimes Q igr)\), let \((X_0,Y_0)\) be the pair of initial positions and \((v_0,B)\) the common source. The first marginal of \(\pi\) is \(\mu\) and the source is independent of \((X_0,Y_0)\), so \((X_0,(v_0,B))\) has law \(\mu\otimes Q\) and \(X_t=\Psi_t(X_0,v_0,B)\) has law \(P^Q_t\mu\); likewise \(Y_t=\Psi_t(Y_0,v_0,B)\) has law \(P^Q_t u\). Hence the law of \((X_t,Y_t)\) is a coupling of the two output laws.

The two solutions have the same input, which cancels in their difference, and the same initial velocity \(v_0\). By the synchronous contraction of the dynamics section (), \(\|X_t-Y_t\|\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\|X_0-Y_0\|\) at every sample point. Squaring, integrating and taking square roots,

\[W_2 igl(P^Q_t\mu,P^Q_t u igr)\le igl(\mathbb E\|X_t-Y_t\|^2 igr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt2e^{-mt/\gamma}\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\pi(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}.\]

Taking the infimum over \(\pi\) gives the claim; the output distance is finite because the right side is. \(\square\)

The common source is what makes the comparison possible without any knowledge of its law: the input is shared by the two copies. No optimal coupling and no stationary law are needed.

KIPLMC/Moments.lean.title: The exact Gaussian velocity norm at particle temperature
KIPLMC/Moments.lean.summary:
In the scaled coordinates each velocity coordinate has the thermal variance \(1/N\): the velocity law is \(\kappa_N=\mathcal N(0,N^{-1}I)\) on \(\mathcal Z_N\), defined in the target section as the image of the standard Gaussian law under \(v\mapsto N^{-1/2}v\). This section proves the reverse identity, that \(\sqrt N\,V\) is standard Gaussian when \(V\) has law \(\kappa_N\), and computes the root mean square norm of a thermal velocity,

\[\bigl(\mathbb E\|V\|^2\bigr)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta+Nd_x}N}=\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta}N+d_x}.\]

This number is the velocity radius that enters the local error of the exponential integrator; it is the source of the factor \(\sqrt{d_\theta/N+d_x}\) in the discretization term of the KIPLMC1 bound, and of the corresponding factor for KIPLMC2.

steps.title: Undoing the thermal scaling of the velocity law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(N>0\). The image of \(\kappa_N\) under \(v\mapsto\sqrt N\,v\) is the standard Gaussian measure \(\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\).

Proof. By definition \(\kappa_N=(s_N)_\#\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\) with \(s_N(v)=(\sqrt N)^{-1}v\). Let \(r_N(v)=\sqrt N\,v\). Both maps are linear, hence continuous and measurable, so the pushforward of a composition is the composition of pushforwards:

\[(r_N)_\#\kappa_N=(r_N)_\#(s_N)_\#\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}=(r_N\circ s_N)_\#\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}.\]

Since \(N>0\), \(\sqrt N\ne0\) and \(r_N(s_N(v))=(\sqrt N\cdot(\sqrt N)^{-1})v=v\), so \(r_N\circ s_N\) is the identity, and the pushforward of a measure by the identity is the measure itself. \(\square\)

This is an equality of measures, so every statement about the law of a standard Gaussian vector, in particular every moment identity, transfers to \(\sqrt N\,V\) when \(V\sim\kappa_N\).

steps.title: The root mean square norm of a thermal velocity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a measure space, \(N>0\), and let \(V\) be a square-integrable random vector with values in \(\mathcal Z_N\) whose law is \(\kappa_N\). Then

\[\|V\|_{L^2}=\Bigl(\int_\Omega\|V\|^2\,d\mathbb P\Bigr)^{1/2}=\sqrt{\frac{d_\theta+Nd_x}N}.\]

Proof. By the previous step, \(\sqrt N\,V=r_N(V)\) has law \((r_N)_\#\kappa_N=\gamma_{\mathcal Z_N}\), the standard Gaussian law on the space \(\mathcal Z_N\) of dimension \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\) (the number of elements of \(I_N\)). For a standard Gaussian vector \(G\) on \(\mathbb R^D\) the coordinates are standard normal, so

\[\mathbb E\|G\|^2=\sum_{a\in I_N}\mathbb E\,G_a^2=D,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad\|G\|_{L^2}=\sqrt D\]

(). Applied to \(G=\sqrt N\,V\) and combined with homogeneity of the \(L^2\) norm and \(\sqrt N>0\), this gives \(\sqrt N\,\|V\|_{L^2}=\sqrt D\). Dividing by \(\sqrt N\) and using \(\sqrt D/\sqrt N=\sqrt{D/N}\) for \(D\ge0\), \(N>0\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

The law of \(V\) is a probability measure, so the hypothesis forces \(\mathbb P(\Omega)=1\). Each of the \(D\) coordinates has variance \(1/N\), and the squared radius \(D/N=d_\theta/N+d_x\) is the sum of these variances. Its square root is the velocity radius at the thermal equilibrium of the particle system; it does not grow with \(N\) when \(d_\theta\) and \(d_x\) are fixed, and the case of zero dimensions is included.

KIPLMC/ReferenceBound.lean.title: The exponential kinetic error bound with a thermal reference
KIPLMC/ReferenceBound.lean.summary:
The first particle algorithm uses exactly the shared exponential step. Its analytical comparison should therefore reuse the same proof. This section applies the shared \(L^{2}\) kinetic theorem to the averaged lifted potential, uses the thermal Gaussian radius, and projects the resulting transport estimate to the MMLE parameter. The result has all three constants in the supplied KIPLMC1 theorem, with the initial supplied coupling cost. Its integral-segment and reference-marginal hypotheses are explicit: construction of a stationary reference and identification of the independent Gaussian chain are still needed for the unconditional sampler theorem.

The conditional comparison displays how the shared local kinetic proof yields initialization, discretization, and concentration terms. Later constructed constructions verify its reference-path and stationary-law requirements.

steps.title: Lift the physical particle force once
steps.body:
The averaged lifted potential \(\bar U_N=V_N/N\) has gradient \(F_N\), the physical-time force. The earlier geometry proves its original smoothness constant \(L\) and strong convexity constant \(m\), independently of particle count. Pointwise application of this Lipschitz gradient defines the force on square-integrable random vectors. It is therefore the particle force on almost-everywhere representatives, with a well-defined square-integrable output. No new exponential update or substitute gradient algorithm is introduced.

The lifted force is still the pointwise gradient of the average potential. Its square-integrable action inherits global Lipschitzness and the same curvature geometry. This permits the shared kinetic local-error proof to be reused without defining a different particle algorithm.

steps.title: Inherit the local comparison, recurrence, and sharp equilibrium term
steps.body:
Let \(S_n\) be numerical phase states and \(R_n\) reference phase states in \(L^{2}\). On each interval, the auxiliary exact path starts at \(S_n\), the reference exact path starts at \(R_n\) and ends at \(R_{n+1}\), and their integral equations have the same additive input. The numerical endpoint is the shared exponential step with velocity noise \(B_h\) and position noise \(\int_0^hB_sds\). Its mild velocity and kinematic identities are explicit inputs. The reference velocity marginal is thermal Gaussian and its position marginal is the normalized lifted Gibbs target.

The thermal moment theorem supplies \(C=\sqrt{(d_\theta+Nd_x)/N}\). steps.title: Find the exact Hessian nullspace
steps.body:
Every term in the second variation is nonnegative when \(\tau\ge0\). If \(\tau>0\), a zero total forces \(w-u=0\) and \(\langle v_j,w\rangle=0\) for every feature. Conversely those equations make every term vanish. The proof isolates the nonnegative prior term, bounds each observation term by the whole sum, and uses strict positivity of every logistic weight to cancel it. If the features span the latent space, orthogonality to every feature extends to their linear span by submodule induction. Taking the inner product with \(w\) itself then gives \(w=0\), and hence \(u=0\). Every nonzero joint direction therefore has strictly positive second variation at each finite state.

Because every finite predictor has a positive logistic weight, zero observation curvature means orthogonality to every feature. Full span eliminates that nullspace at each finite state. This is a pointwise positive-definiteness statement; it does not provide a positive lower eigenvalue uniformly over all states.
